### 2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 10 · 12 marks

<span class="tag">Two curves</span><span class="tag">Asymptotes</span><span class="tag">Stationary points</span>

The curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ have equations

$$
C_1:\ y=\frac{ax}{x+5},
\qquad
C_2:\ y=\frac{x^2+(a+10)x+5a+26}{x+5},
$$

respectively, where $a>2$.

**(i)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C_1$. **[2]**

**(ii)** Find the equation of the oblique asymptote of $C_2$. **[2]**

**(iii)** Show that $C_1$ and $C_2$ do not intersect. **[2]**

**(iv)** Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $C_2$. **[3]**

**(v)** Sketch $C_1$ and $C_2$ on a single diagram. You do not need to calculate the coordinates of any points where $C_2$ crosses the axes. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(i)** Since

$$
\frac{ax}{x+5}=a-\frac{5a}{x+5},
$$

the asymptotes of $C_1$ are

$$
\boxed{x=-5},\qquad\boxed{y=a}.
$$

**(ii)** For $C_2$,

$$
x^2+(a+10)x+5a+26=(x+5)(x+a+5)+1,
$$

so its oblique asymptote is

$$
\boxed{y=x+a+5}.
$$

**(iii)** Equating the two functions and multiplying by $x+5$ gives

$$
x^2+10x+5a+26=0.
$$

Its discriminant is

$$
100-4(5a+26)=-4-20a<0,
$$

so the curves do not intersect.

**(iv)** Since $C_2$ is $y=x+a+5+1/(x+5)$,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac1{(x+5)^2}.
$$

Thus the stationary-point equation

$$
x^2+10x+24=0,
$$

hence the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(-4,a+2),\quad(-6,a-2)}.
$$

The sketch must show the common vertical asymptote $x=-5$, the stated horizontal/oblique asymptotes, the two stationary points of $C_2$, and no intersection between the curves.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2019-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q10; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q10.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #rational-2019-mj-13}
### 2019 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Oblique asymptote</span><span class="tag">Stationary points</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2}{kx-1},
$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

**(i)** Obtain the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(ii)** Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $C$. **[3]**

**(iii)** Sketch $C$. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(i)** Long division gives

$$
\frac{x^2}{kx-1}=\frac{x}{k}+\frac1{k^2}+\frac{1/k^2}{kx-1}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac1k},
\qquad
\boxed{y=\frac{x}{k}+\frac1{k^2}}.
$$

Also

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(kx-2)}{(kx-1)^2},
$$

so the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(0,0)},
\qquad
\boxed{\left(\frac2k,\frac4{k^2}\right)}.
$$

The branch containing the origin touches the $x$-axis at $(0,0)$; the other branch has its minimum at $\left(2/k,4/k^2\right)$. Both branches approach the stated asymptotes.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2019-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2019, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2019 October/November · 9231/11, 9231/12 & 9231/13 · Question 4 · 7 marks

<span class="tag">Given asymptote</span><span class="tag">Unknown constants</span>

The line $y=2x+1$ is an asymptote of the curve $C$ with equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+1}{ax+b}.
$$

**(i)** Find the values of $a$ and $b$. **[3]**

**(ii)** State the equation of the other asymptote of $C$. **[1]**

**(iii)** Sketch $C$, indicating the coordinates of any point of intersection with the $y$-axis. You do not need to find the stationary points. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(i)** Write $x^2+1=(ax+b)(2x+1)+R$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$ and $x$ gives $2a=1$ and $a+2b=0$. Hence

$$
\boxed{a=\frac12},\qquad\boxed{b=-\frac14}.
$$

The other asymptote is

$$
\boxed{x=\frac12}.
$$

The $y$-intercept is

$$
\boxed{(0,-4)}.
$$

The two branches approach $x=\frac12$ and $y=2x+1$ with the correct signs; the numerator has no real zero, so the curve does not cross the $x$-axis.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2019-on"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2019, Q4; 9231/12/O/N/2019, Q4; 9231/13/O/N/2019, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 1 · 6 marks

<span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

Let $a$ be a positive constant.

**(a)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{ax}{x+7}.
$$

**[2]**

**(b)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{ax}{x+7}\right|
$$

and find the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{ax}{x+7}\right|>\frac a2.
$$

**[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $ax/(x+7)=a-7a/(x+7)$, the original curve has asymptotes $x=-7$ and $y=a$, and passes through $(0,0)$.

**(b)** The function is negative on $-7<x<0$, so reflect precisely this part in the $x$-axis to obtain the modulus graph.

The critical equations are

$$
\frac{ax}{x+7}=\pm\frac a2,
$$

giving $x=7$ and $x=-\frac73$. A sign chart across $-7,-7/3,7$ then gives

$$
\boxed{x<-7\quad\text{or}\quad-7<x<-\frac73\quad\text{or}\quad x>7}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2020-mj-11-12-q1"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q1; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 3 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Oblique asymptote</span><span class="tag">Stationary points</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2}{2x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of the stationary points on $C$. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Long division gives

$$
\frac{x^2}{2x+1}=\frac x2-\frac14+\frac{1/4}{2x+1}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-\frac12},
\qquad
\boxed{y=\frac x2-\frac14}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{2x(2x+1)-2x^2}{(2x+1)^2}
=\frac{2x(x+1)}{(2x+1)^2}.
$$

Thus $x=0,-1$, giving the stationary points

$$
\boxed{(0,0)},\qquad\boxed{(-1,-1)}.
$$

The right branch touches the $x$-axis at the origin; the left branch has a stationary point at $(-1,-1)$. Both branches approach the stated asymptotes.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2020-mj-11-12-q3"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q3; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">No turning points</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{10+x-2x^2}{2x-3}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that $C$ has no turning points. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{10+x-2x^2}{2x-3}\right|
$$

and find in exact form the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{10+x-2x^2}{2x-3}\right|<4.
$$

**[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Since

$$
\frac{10+x-2x^2}{2x-3}=-x-1+\frac7{2x-3},
$$

the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac32},\qquad\boxed{y=-x-1}.
$$

**(b)** Differentiation gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-1-\frac{14}{(2x-3)^2}<0,
$$

so there are no turning points. **(c)** Since

$$
10+x-2x^2=-(2x-5)(x+2),
$$

the intersections are

$$
\boxed{(-2,0),\quad\left(\frac52,0\right),\quad\left(0,-\frac{10}{3}\right)}.
$$

**(d)** For the modulus graph, reflect all negative parts in the $x$-axis. The boundary equations are

$$
f(x)=4\Longrightarrow 2x^2+7x-22=0,
$$

$$
f(x)=-4\Longrightarrow 2x^2-9x+2=0.
$$

Using their exact roots and a sign chart gives

$$
\boxed{-\frac{11}{2}<x<\frac{9-\sqrt{65}}4
\quad\text{or}\quad
2<x<\frac{9+\sqrt{65}}4}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2020-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2020, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 6 · 12 marks

<span class="tag">Range</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+x-1}{x-1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that there is no point on $C$ for which $1<y<5$. **[4]**

**(c)** Find the coordinates of the intersections of $C$ with the axes, and sketch $C$. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x^2+x-1}{x-1}\right|.
$$

**[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Since

$$
\frac{x^2+x-1}{x-1}=x+2+\frac1{x-1},
$$

the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=1},\qquad\boxed{y=x+2}.
$$

**(b)** Rearranging as a quadratic in $x$ gives

$$
x^2+(1-y)x+y-1=0.
$$

The discriminant is

$$
\Delta=(1-y)^2-4(y-1)=(y-1)(y-5).
$$

It is negative precisely for $1<y<5$, proving the statement. **(c)** The intersections are

$$
\boxed{\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt5}{2},0\right),
\quad\left(\frac{-1-\sqrt5}{2},0\right),
\quad(0,1)}.
$$

For the modulus graph, reflect all portions below the $x$-axis in the $x$-axis, producing cusps at both roots.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2020-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2020, Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2020, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 6 · 13 marks

<span class="tag">Square</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Comparison</span>

Let $a$ be a positive constant. The curves $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_3$ have equations

$$
C_1:\ y=\frac{x-a}{x-2a},
$$

$$
C_2:\ y=\left(\frac{x-a}{x-2a}\right)^2,
\qquad
C_3:\ y=\left|\frac{x-a}{x-2a}\right|.
$$

**(a)** Sketch $C_1$. **[2]**

**(b)(i)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points of $C_2$. **[3]**

**(b)(ii)** Find the coordinates of any intersections of $C_2$ and $C_3$. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C_2$ and $C_3$ on a single diagram, clearly identifying each curve. Hence solve

$$
\left(\frac{x-a}{x-2a}\right)^2
\le
\left|\frac{x-a}{x-2a}\right|.
$$

**[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$C_1$ has asymptotes $x=2a$ and $y=1$, and passes through $(a,0)$ and $\left(0,\frac12\right)$.

**(b)(i)** Let $g(x)=(x-a)/(x-2a)$. Since

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\{g(x)^2\}=2g(x)g'(x),
\qquad
g'(x)=\frac{-a}{(x-2a)^2},
$$

$C_2$ has the stationary point

$$
\boxed{(a,0)}.
$$

**(b)(ii)** Put $u=|g(x)|\ge0$. Then $C_2=C_3$ when $u^2=u$, so $u=0$ or $1$, giving

$$
\boxed{(a,0),\qquad\left(\frac{3a}{2},1\right)}.
$$

**(c)** The inequality is $u^2\le u$, i.e. $0\le u\le1$. Solving $|g(x)|\le1$, or reading the relative positions from the sketches, gives

$$
\boxed{x\le\frac{3a}{2}}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2020-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2020, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 7 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Oblique asymptote</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+x+9}{x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of the stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x^2+x+9}{x+1}\right|
$$

and solve

$$
2|x^2+x+9|>13|x+1|.
$$

**[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=x}.
$$

Since $y=x+9/(x+1)$,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac9{(x+1)^2}
=\frac{(x-2)(x+4)}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Thus the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(2,5),\qquad(-4,-7)}.
$$

The curve has $y$-intercept $(0,9)$ and no $x$-intercepts. Reflect the negative branch in the $x$-axis for the modulus graph.

The boundary equations give $x=\frac12$ and $x=5$; the other quadratic has no real roots. Therefore

$$
\boxed{x<\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad x>5}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2021-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2021, Q7; 9231/12/M/J/2021, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 7 · 14 marks

<span class="tag">Two vertical asymptotes</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2-x-3}{1+x-x^2}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x^2-x-3}{1+x-x^2}\right|
$$

and find in exact form the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{x^2-x-3}{1+x-x^2}\right|<3.
$$

**[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{x=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{y=-1}.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4x-2}{(1+x-x^2)^2}.
$$

Thus $x=1/2$ and the stationary point is

$$
\boxed{\left(\frac12,-\frac{13}{5}\right)}.
$$

The intersections are

$$
\boxed{\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{13}}2,0\right),
\quad\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}2,0\right),
\quad(0,-3)}.
$$

For the inequality, solve $f(x)=\pm3$ and use the modulus sketch. The result is

$$
\boxed{x<\frac{1-\sqrt7}{2}
\quad\text{or}\quad
0<x<1
\quad\text{or}\quad
x>\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2021-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2021, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Horizontal asymptote</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{4x+5}{4-4x^2}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{4x+5}{4-4x^2}\right|
$$

and solve

$$
4|4x+5|>5|4-4x^2|.
$$

**[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{x=1},\qquad\boxed{y=0}.
$$

The derivative numerator factorises as $2(2x+1)(x+2)$, so the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{\left(-2,\frac14\right),\qquad\left(-\frac12,1\right)}.
$$

The intersections are

$$
\boxed{\left(-\frac54,0\right),\qquad\left(0,\frac54\right)}.
$$

Solving $|f(x)|=\frac54$ and reading the required regions from the modulus graph gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{2-3\sqrt6}{5}<x<-\frac45
\quad\text{or}\quad
0<x<\frac{2+3\sqrt6}{5},
\qquad x\ne\pm1}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2021-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2021, Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2021, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 6 · 14 marks

<span class="tag">Range</span><span class="tag">Graph comparison</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2}{x-3}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that there is no point on $C$ for which $0<y<12$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$. **[2]**

**(d)(i)** Sketch $y=x^2/(x-3)$ and $y=x-3$ on one diagram, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[4]**

**(d)(ii)** Use the sketch to find the set of values of $c$ for which

$$
\frac{x^2}{x-3}\le x+c
$$

has no solution. **[1]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=3},\qquad\boxed{y=x+3}.
$$

Writing the equation as

$$
x^2-yx+3y=0
$$

shows that real $x$ requires $y^2-12y\ge0$. Hence the range is $y\le0$ or $y\ge12$.

The rational curve touches the axes at $(0,0)$. The line $y=x-3$ meets the axes at $(3,0)$ and $(0,-3)$. From the relative positions of the graphs,

$$
\boxed{c\le-3}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2021-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2021, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2022 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 5 · 12 marks

<span class="tag">No vertical asymptote</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{2x^2-x-1}{x^2+x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $C$ has no vertical asymptotes and state its horizontal asymptote. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of the stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{2x^2-x-1}{x^2+x+1}\right|
$$

and state the set of values of $k$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{2x^2-x-1}{x^2+x+1}\right|=k
$$

has four distinct real solutions. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$x^2+x+1$ has discriminant $-3$, so it has no real zeros and there are no vertical asymptotes. The horizontal asymptote is

$$
\boxed{y=2}.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3x(x+2)}{(x^2+x+1)^2}.
$$

Thus the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(0,-1),\qquad(-2,3)}.
$$

The intersections are

$$
\boxed{(1,0),\qquad\left(-\frac12,0\right),\qquad(0,-1)}.
$$

After reflecting the negative part in the $x$-axis, a horizontal line meets the modulus graph four times precisely when

$$
\boxed{0<k<1}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2022-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2022, Q5; 9231/12/M/J/2022, Q5.</div>
:::

### 2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 6 marks

<span class="tag">$f(|x|)$</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

**(a)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{x+1}{x-1}.
$$

**[2]**

**(b)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{|x|+1}{|x|-1}
$$

and find the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac{|x|+1}{|x|-1}<-2.
$$

**[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The original graph has asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=1$, and intersections $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$.

For the second graph, keep the part for $x\ge0$ and reflect it in the $y$-axis. Solving the inequality in terms of $|x|$ gives

$$
\boxed{-1<x<-\frac13
\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac13<x<1}.
$$

</details>

### 2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Oblique asymptote</span><span class="tag">Range</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{ax^2+x-1}{x-1},
$$

where $a$ is a positive constant.

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that there is no point on $C$ for which $1<y<1+4a$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$. You do not need to find the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=1},\qquad\boxed{y=ax+a+1}.
$$

Rearranging gives

$$
ax^2-(y-1)x+(y-1)=0.
$$

No real $x$ occurs when

$$
(y-1)^2-4a(y-1)<0,
$$

which is precisely $1<y<1+4a$. Equivalently, the turning points are $(0,1)$ and $(2,4a+1)$, lying on separate branches. The sketch must show both branches in the correct positions relative to $x=1$ and $y=ax+a+1$.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2022-mj-13-q3"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2022, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2023 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Reciprocal graph</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation $y=f(x)$, where

$$
f(x)=\frac{x^2+2}{x^2-x-2}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac1{f(x)}.
$$

**[2]**

**(e)** Find the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac1{f(x)}<f(x).
$$

**[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes of $C$ are

$$
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{x=2},\qquad\boxed{y=1}.
$$

The stationary points are approximately

$$
\boxed{(-8.2,0.9),\qquad(0.2,-0.9)}.
$$

The only axis intersection is

$$
\boxed{(0,-1)}.
$$

For $y=1/f(x)$, the original vertical asymptotes become open points on the $x$-axis, the horizontal asymptote remains $y=1$, and the original function has no roots, so the reciprocal graph has no vertical asymptote arising from a root.

Solving the boundary equations $f(x)=\pm1$ gives $x=-4,0,\frac12$. The required set is

$$
\boxed{-4<x<-1
\quad\text{or}\quad
0<x<\frac12
\quad\text{or}\quad
x>2}.
$$

</details>

<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2023, Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2023, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 7 · 16 marks

<span class="tag">Reciprocal graph</span><span class="tag">Stationary point</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation $y=f(x)$, where

$$
f(x)=\frac{x^2}{x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[2]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$. **[3]**

**(d)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on

$$
y=\frac1{f(x)}.
$$

**[2]**

**(e)** Sketch $y=1/f(x)$ and find, in exact form, the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac1{f(x)}>f(x).
$$

**[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

For $C$, the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=x-1},
$$

and the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(0,0),\qquad(-2,-4)}.
$$

Since

$$
\frac1{f(x)}=\frac{x+1}{x^2},
$$

its stationary point is

$$
\boxed{\left(-2,-\frac14\right)}.
$$

The reciprocal graph has a vertical asymptote $x=0$, horizontal asymptote $y=0$, and an open point at $(-1,0)$. Solving $f(x)=\pm1$ gives $x=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$, and the inequality gives

$$
\boxed{x<-1
\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}<x<\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\qquad x\ne0}.
$$

</details>

### 2024 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 6 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Parameter</span><span class="tag">No stationary points</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+ax+1}{x+2},
$$

where $a>\frac52$.

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that $C$ has no stationary points. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the point of intersection with the $y$-axis and labelling the asymptotes. **[3]**

**(d)(i)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x^2+ax+1}{x+2}\right|.
$$

**[2]**

**(d)(ii)** On the same sketch, draw the line $y=a$. **[1]**

**(d)(iii)** It is given that

$$
\left|\frac{x^2+ax+1}{x+2}\right|<a
$$

for

$$
-5-\sqrt{14}<x<-3
\quad\text{and}\quad
-5+\sqrt{14}<x<3.
$$

Find $a$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Long division gives

$$
\frac{x^2+ax+1}{x+2}=x+a-2+\frac{5-2a}{x+2}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-2},\qquad\boxed{y=x+a-2}.
$$

Differentiation gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac{2a-5}{(x+2)^2}>0,
$$

so there are no stationary points. The $y$-intercept is

$$
\boxed{\left(0,\frac12\right)}.
$$

Reflect the negative portions to obtain the modulus graph and add the horizontal line $y=a$. The stated boundary values agree with the equations $f(x)=\pm a$ only when

$$
\boxed{a=5}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2024-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2024, Q6; 9231/12/M/J/2024, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 13 marks

<span class="tag">No vertical asymptote</span><span class="tag">$y^2=f(x)$</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x+1}{x^2+3}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $C$ has no vertical asymptotes and state its horizontal asymptote. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y^2=\frac{x+1}{x^2+3},
$$

stating the coordinates of the stationary points and intersections with the axes. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$x^2+3$ has no real zero, so there is no vertical asymptote. The horizontal asymptote is

$$
\boxed{y=0}.
$$

Using the quotient rule,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{x^2+3-2x(x+1)}{(x^2+3)^2}
=\frac{-(x-1)(x+3)}{(x^2+3)^2}.
$$

Thus the stationary points of $C$ are

$$
\boxed{\left(-3,-\frac16\right),\qquad\left(1,\frac12\right)}.
$$

Its intersections are

$$
\boxed{(-1,0),\qquad\left(0,\frac13\right)}.
$$

For $y^2=f(x)$, real points occur only for $x\ge-1$ and the graph is symmetrical about the $x$-axis. Its stationary points are

$$
\boxed{\left(1,\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),\qquad
\left(1,-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)},
$$

and its axis intersections are

$$
\boxed{(-1,0),\qquad
\left(0,\frac1{\sqrt3}\right),\qquad
\left(0,-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2024-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2024, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2024 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 6 · 13 marks

<span class="tag">Three branches</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{4x^2+x+1}{2x^2-7x+3}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes. **[5]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{4x^2+x+1}{2x^2-7x+3}\right|
$$

and state the set of values of $k$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{4x^2+x+1}{2x^2-7x+3}\right|=k
$$

has four distinct real solutions. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac12},\qquad\boxed{x=3},\qquad\boxed{y=2}.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{-10(3x+1)(x-1)}{(2x^2-7x+3)^2}.
$$

Hence the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{\left(-\frac13,\frac15\right),\qquad(1,-3)}.
$$

The numerator has no real roots; the only axis intersection is

$$
\boxed{\left(0,\frac13\right)}.
$$

The graph has three branches separated by the two vertical asymptotes. After reflecting the negative parts in the $x$-axis, four distinct intersections with $y=k$ occur when

$$
\boxed{k>3}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2024-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2024, Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2024, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 6 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Range</span><span class="tag">Reciprocal graph</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+3}{x^2+1}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $C$ has no vertical asymptotes and state its horizontal asymptote. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that $1<y\le3$ for all real $x$. **[4]**

**(c)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[2]**

**(d)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes and labelling the asymptote. **[3]**

**(e)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{x^2+1}{x^2+3}
$$

and find the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac{x^2+1}{x^2+3}<\frac12.
$$

**[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

There are no vertical asymptotes and the horizontal asymptote is

$$
\boxed{y=1}.
$$

Writing

$$
y=1+\frac2{x^2+1}
$$

shows immediately that $1<y\le3$. Also

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{4x}{(x^2+1)^2},
$$

so the only stationary point and axis intersection is

$$
\boxed{(0,3)}.
$$

The reciprocal graph is symmetrical about the $y$-axis, has horizontal asymptote $y=1$, and minimum $\left(0,\frac13\right)$. The inequality gives

$$
\boxed{-1<x<1}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 7 · 15 marks

<span class="tag">Two vertical asymptotes</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{2x^2-5x}{2x^2-7x-4}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{2x^2-5x}{2x^2-7x-4}\right|.
$$

**[1]**

**(e)** Find in exact form the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{2x^2-5x}{2x^2-7x-4}\right|<\frac19.
$$

**[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Since $2x^2-7x-4=(2x+1)(x-4)$ and the ratio of leading coefficients is $1$, the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-\frac12},\qquad\boxed{x=4},\qquad\boxed{y=1}.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{-4(x+5)(x-1)}{(2x^2-7x-4)^2}.
$$

Therefore the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{\left(-5,\frac{25}{27}\right),\qquad\left(1,\frac13\right)}.
$$

The intersections are

$$
\boxed{(0,0),\qquad\left(\frac52,0\right)}.
$$

The boundary equations are $9(2x^2-5x)=\pm(2x^2-7x-4)$. Solving both quadratics and using a sign chart gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{13-3\sqrt{21}}{10}<x<\frac{19-3\sqrt{33}}{16}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac{19+3\sqrt{33}}{16}<x<\frac{13+3\sqrt{21}}{10}}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2025-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2025, Q7; 9231/12/M/J/2025, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 14 marks

<span class="tag">Parameter</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+a}{x+a},
$$

where $a$ is a positive constant.

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find, in terms of $a$, the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points on $C$. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}\right|.
$$

**[1]**

**(e)** Find the set of values of $a$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}\right|=a
$$

has two real solutions. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Long division gives

$$
\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}=x-a+\frac{a^2+a}{x+a}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=-a},\qquad\boxed{y=x-a}.
$$

Also

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac{a^2+a}{(x+a)^2}.
$$

Setting this equal to zero gives the stationary-point $x$-coordinates

$$
\boxed{x=-a\pm\sqrt{a^2+a}}.
$$

The numerator has no real zero and the $y$-intercept is

$$
\boxed{(0,1)}.
$$

For $|f(x)|=a$, the equation $f(x)=-a$ becomes

$$
x^2+ax+a+a^2=0,
$$

whose discriminant is $-3a^2-4a<0$. The equation $f(x)=a$ becomes

$$
x^2-ax+a-a^2=0,
$$

and has two distinct real roots when

$$
5a^2-4a>0.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{a>\frac45}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2025-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2025, Q6.</div>
:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 7 · 16 marks

<span class="tag">Range</span><span class="tag">$f(|x|)$</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+x-4}{x^2+x+2}.
$$

**(a)** State the equation of the asymptote of $C$. **[1]**

**(b)** Show that, for all real $x$,

$$
-\frac{17}{7}\le y<1.
$$

**[4]**

**(c)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points of $C$. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(e)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{|x|^2+|x|-4}{|x|^2+|x|+2}
$$

and find the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac{|x|^2+|x|-4}{|x|^2+|x|+2}< -\frac12.
$$

**[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptote is

$$
\boxed{y=1}.
$$

Since

$$
y=1-\frac6{x^2+x+2}
$$

and

$$
x^2+x+2=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+\frac74\ge\frac74,
$$

it follows directly that

$$
\boxed{-\frac{17}{7}\le y<1}.
$$

Furthermore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{6(2x+1)}{(x^2+x+2)^2},
$$

so the stationary point is

$$
\boxed{\left(-\frac12,-\frac{17}{7}\right)}.
$$

The intersections are

$$
\boxed{(0,-2),\quad
\left(\frac{-1-\sqrt{17}}2,0\right),\quad
\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}2,0\right)}.
$$

For $f(|x|)$, retain the $x\ge0$ half of $C$ and reflect it in the $y$-axis. Put $u=|x|$. Then

$$
1-\frac6{u^2+u+2}< -\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^2+u-2<0.
$$

Since $u\ge0$, this gives $0\le u<1$, hence

$$
\boxed{-1<x<1}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2025-mj-14"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/14/M/J/2025, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 14 marks

<span class="tag">No stationary points</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that $C$ has no stationary points. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}\right|.
$$

**[2]**

**(e)** Find in exact form the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\left|\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}\right|>2.
$$

**[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

The asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac{-3-\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{x=\frac{-3+\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{y=0}.
$$

Differentiation gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=-\frac{x^2+4x+5}{(x^2+3x+1)^2}.
$$

The numerator quadratic has discriminant $16-20=-4<0$ and is always positive, so the derivative is never zero. Hence there are no stationary points. The intersections are

$$
\boxed{(-2,0),\qquad(0,2)}.
$$

Solving the boundary equations $f(x)=\pm2$ and reading the intervals from the modulus sketch gives

$$
\boxed{
-\frac74-\frac{\sqrt{17}}4<x<-\frac52
\quad\text{or}\quad
-\frac74+\frac{\sqrt{17}}4<x<0,
\qquad
x\ne\frac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2025-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2025, Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2025, Q7.</div>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 7 · 14 marks

<span class="tag">Oblique asymptote</span><span class="tag">$f(|x|)$</span><span class="tag">Inequality</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{x^2+x+1}{x+1}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$. **[3]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\frac{|x|^2+|x|+1}{|x|+1}.
$$

**[2]**

**(e)** Find, in exact form, the set of values of $x$ for which

$$
\frac{|x|^2+|x|+1}{|x|+1}<3.
$$

**[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Long division gives

$$
\frac{x^2+x+1}{x+1}=x+\frac1{x+1}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes of $C$ are

$$
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=x}.
$$

Also

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac1{(x+1)^2}=0
$$

gives $x=0,-2$, so the stationary points are

$$
\boxed{(0,1),\qquad(-2,-3)}.
$$

For $f(|x|)$, retain the right-hand branch and reflect it in the $y$-axis; the result is smooth at $(0,1)$. Put $u=|x|$. Then

$$
\frac{u^2+u+1}{u+1}<3
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^2-2u-2<0.
$$

Thus $0\le u<1+\sqrt3$, giving

$$
\boxed{-1-\sqrt3<x<1+\sqrt3}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="rational-2025-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2025, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 7 · 16 marks

<span class="tag">No stationary points</span><span class="tag">Modulus</span><span class="tag">Given intervals</span>

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
y=\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}.
$$

**(a)** Find the equations of the asymptotes of $C$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that $C$ has no stationary points. **[4]**

**(c)** Sketch $C$, stating the coordinates of the points of intersection with the axes. **[3]**

**(d)** Sketch

$$
y=\left|\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}\right|.
$$

**[2]**

**(e)** Given that

$$
\left|\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}\right|<4
$$

for

$$
\frac{-29-\sqrt{4441}}{20}<x<p
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{-29+\sqrt{4441}}{20}<x<q,
$$

find $p$ and $q$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Long division gives

$$
\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}
=x+\frac7{10}-\frac{27/5}{10x-18}.
$$

Hence the asymptotes are

$$
\boxed{x=\frac95},\qquad\boxed{y=x+\frac7{10}}.
$$

Differentiating this form,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac{54}{(10x-18)^2}>0,
$$

so there are no stationary points. The intersections are

$$
\boxed{(0,1),\qquad\left(-\frac9{10},0\right),\qquad(2,0)}.
$$

For $|f(x)|<4$, the four boundary values come from $f(x)=4$ and $f(x)=-4$. The two values represented by $p,q$ come from $f(x)=4$, giving

$$
10x^2-51x+54=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{p=\frac32},\qquad\boxed{q=\frac{18}{5}}.
$$

</details>
